items.title: Fireworks AI's October breach widens to customer secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights — Notion disconnects, disables Insights; Cursor and Harvey also named
items.summary: On November 9, 2026, inference platform Fireworks AI expanded the disclosure of its second October security incident. In the updated bulletin, the company said an unauthorized party reached stored secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights for a limited set of accounts, along with customer billing and account data more broadly. The access path was a compromise of an unnamed third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks' R&D machines on October 23, with an unauthorized workload running on Fireworks development machines on October 24. This is distinct from an earlier October incident — first disclosed on roughly October 6 and investigated by Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 — in which an unauthorized party used internal Fireworks credentials to reach environment variables holding API keys and tokens for a limited number of customer accounts. Fireworks has attributed the new activity to an actor it believes is linked to the financially-motivated 'LLMJacking' trend — stealing inference credentials to run paid workloads on the victim's account. Payment card numbers were not exposed; Fireworks does not store them. Three named customers are working with Fireworks on impact assessment: Notion, Cursor, and legal-AI company Harvey. Notion's own advisory (vendor notice November 2 or November 6 depending on source; Notion-side action timestamps November 3) says fewer than 1% of its workspaces may have been affected — specifically unattributable Notion AI chat sessions used for its Insights feature. Notion has disabled Insights, disconnected from Fireworks (November 3), deleted its data at Fireworks, stopped all data and traffic, halted all training runs, and stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks. Workspace owners can review affected data through an in-product security-incident review page available on desktop and web (not mobile), accessible only to workspaces with managed members. Harvey says none of its data was affected. Cursor-specific impact has not been publicly confirmed. Fireworks has also disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training while the investigation continues. Its Inference service, Training SDK, and Nexus — which keep no customer data by default — appear not to have been impacted, though the investigation is ongoing. Fireworks has not disclosed the identity of the cloud provider, the exact number of affected files or customers, or how the internal credentials used in the first incident were obtained. Reporting also mentions that some large-spend customers are reportedly considering alternative providers, though the sourcing is anonymous.
items.why_it_matters: This matters for anyone who builds on hosted AI infrastructure, which now effectively means anyone writing agents on top of a model API. Three practical threads. First, the supply-chain-blast-radius is the real lesson. A single compromised cloud host at Fireworks has now reached billing data, secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights at a vendor whose named customer list includes Notion (writing and knowledge work), Cursor (developer coding), and Harvey (legal). That is three different verticals downstream of one upstream failure. The pattern — a shared inference platform becoming the single point of compromise for downstream apps that assume they are serving their own users — is the thing to internalize. Any Python agent calling a hosted model endpoint sits inside a similar dependency graph, and the mitigation is the same regardless of which inference provider is in the hot seat this week: rotate keys at any inference vendor you have ever sent data to, keep a second provider warm, and assume logs are sometimes retained even when zero-retention is the headline marketing claim. Second, Notion's response is a useful reference design worth studying. Within days of the vendor notice, Notion disabled the affected feature (Insights), terminated the vendor connection, deleted its data at the vendor, stopped all training runs through the vendor, stopped serving open-weight models through the vendor, and surfaced the incident to workspace owners through an in-product review page. That is a clean chain of actions, and the separation between the user-facing feature and the vendor relationship is the architectural choice that made the fast cutover possible. If you are designing a product that sends user data to a hosted model, build it so the vendor can be swapped or turned off at the feature level — not only as a whole-product migration — and keep a plain-English description of what data each vendor sees. Third, the 'LLMJacking' framing is the piece worth knowing about by name. The attacker profile Fireworks describes is not a nation-state or an espionage operator; it is a financially-motivated group stealing inference credentials to resell compute or run paid workloads on the victim's account. For a hobbyist with a $20/month ChatGPT or Claude subscription that is background noise. For anyone with a corporate OpenAI/Anthropic/Together/Fireworks key stored in a .env file, a GitHub Actions secret, or a shared config, LLMJacking is now the realistic threat model — more likely than targeted data exfiltration. The practical steps: rotate the key, scope it narrowly (project-level rather than account-level where providers allow), enable per-key spend limits, and watch for unexpected usage spikes. Notion's bulletin also mentions rotating any secrets that may have ended up inside an AI chat with the platform, which is a good reminder that chat logs with AI assistants are secret-material by default and should be treated that way.
items.why_it_matters_brief: A single compromised cloud host at Fireworks hit Notion, Cursor, and Harvey through one dependency — LLMJacking is now the real threat model for anyone storing inference keys in a .env file.

items.title: Anthropic's amended S-1 reports $16.96B Q3 revenue — roughly 1.7x OpenAI's reported $10B Q3, the first filed data point where a frontier-lab revenue leaderboard flips
items.summary: Anthropic's amended S-1 filing (S-1/A), dated November 10, 2026, reports approximately $16.96 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q3) — up roughly 47% quarter-over-quarter from Q2 — and a Q3 operating loss of about $567 million. The same filing sets the proposed IPO range at $70 to $78 per share across 825 million shares, implying a top-of-range raise around $64.35 billion and a valuation in the broad neighborhood of $1.0 trillion to $1.4 trillion, depending on the valuation method used (reporting varies: ABC News cites ~$1.3 trillion; other outlets cite ranges between ~$1.0 trillion and ~$1.4 trillion). Anthropic will trade as 'ANT' on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, with pricing expected in the week of November 16 to 19. A special Class F share held through an entity controlled by Anthropic's seven co-founders represents 50.1% of overall shareholder voting power, preserving founder control post-IPO. The Q3 figure sits alongside a reported (but not filed) OpenAI Q3 revenue of approximately $10 billion, surfaced by The Information and relayed through FirstSquawk and Yahoo Finance; OpenAI is private and does not file revenue with the SEC, so this is secondary reporting rather than a filed number. The direct comparison is imperfect in one important way: Anthropic's S-1/A states that it recognizes cloud-marketplace revenue on a gross basis, which inflates headline revenue relative to a net-of-reseller-cut accounting method; CNBC's coverage flags that Anthropic and OpenAI account for cloud-marketplace sales differently. On an apples-to-apples basis, the gap would narrow, though direction of advantage likely still holds. Two further signals from the filing and surrounding coverage are worth noting. First, commentary citing the filing surfaces approximately $895 billion in multi-year compute commitments and roughly 900% net revenue retention (SaaStr) — both of which, if accurate, are the primary explanations for the Q3 revenue jump: dollar-expansion from the existing enterprise base rather than net-new-logo growth. Second, CNBC-sourced reporting (relayed via FourWeekMBA) says the roadshow book was already covered at the $70-$78 range on day one, and that institutional demand was described as stronger than the comparison point of SpaceX's June IPO book at the same stage; a parallel Reuters-sourced report says investors have voiced doubts about the schedule. Both reads cannot be true; expect the pricing level (top of range, below range, or above) to surface which signal was closer.
items.why_it_matters: This is one of the quieter big stories of the week because the data point lands in a filing rather than through a product launch. Three threads worth noticing. First, this is the first public-filing data point where a frontier-lab revenue leaderboard has flipped. Anthropic has been the smaller-revenue lab in nearly every public comparison for three years — behind OpenAI on consumer usage, behind OpenAI on total revenue. A filed $16.96 billion Q3 against OpenAI's reported $10 billion Q3 is the first filing-grade reading that puts Anthropic ahead. The structural explanation appears to be enterprise contract concentration: the roughly 900% net revenue retention figure cited by SaaStr implies very high dollar-expansion within an established enterprise customer base, and Claude Code specifically has been earning higher per-seat ARR than ChatGPT consumer subscriptions since mid-2026. The counter-signal is the accounting-basis caveat: on a net-of-cloud-reseller-cut basis, the comparison is likely tighter than 1.7x, and OpenAI probably still leads on consumer-facing monetization when ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscriptions are included. Read both numbers as directionally correct but not literal head-to-head totals. Second, the $567 million Q3 operating loss is the sleeper detail. If accurate, Anthropic is losing roughly 3.3% on each revenue dollar at Q3 scale. OpenAI's Q1 operating margin was reported at approximately negative 122%, and Q2 was reportedly worse — the structural gap in unit economics between the two labs is probably the single most important fact in frontier AI right now. It means Anthropic can plausibly raise capital at IPO-grade valuations with a visible path to self-funding, while OpenAI's capital needs keep scaling with revenue growth. For Gabe, this matters because it is the first filing-grade evidence that frontier labs can run as real businesses at $10 billion-plus quarterly scale, not as growth-fueled science projects. The Claude Code pricing structure ($20 Pro, $100 Max, $200 Max+) that Anthropic has been quietly stable on all year is probably the unit-economics story — and it is the pricing book worth paying attention to for anyone who wants a sustainable AI-coding subscription over the next 12 months. Third, the pricing window is the one to watch: November 18-19 is the operative date, with trading expected the week of November 16 and no later than before Thanksgiving. The $70-$78 range at 825 million shares puts the raise at $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion, which — if hit — would be one of the five largest IPOs in history. The specific signal to watch is not the pricing level in dollars, but how the gross-versus-net cloud-marketplace accounting question lands in analyst models. That accounting method is now the reference framework for how every future private-market AI-company valuation gets debated. If buyers accept the gross-basis reading, Anthropic prices at or above the top of the range; if buyers push back and insist on net-of-reseller-cut, pricing lands at $70 or below. Either outcome sets the vocabulary for the next 12-24 months of AI-company valuation conversations.
